title: The Man Who Ended World Hunger
description:
What if one chemical reaction is the reason billions of people are alive today? This is the story of the Haber process (Haber-Bosch process) — the invention that pulled nitrogen from thin air, created synthetic fertilizer, and saved humanity from mass famine. Without it, experts estimate today’s population would be closer to 1.5 billion instead of 8.5 billion.

In this video, Pale Blue Thoughts traces the journey of Fritz Haber, from his early struggles to his breakthrough in 1909: using iron catalysts, 450°C temperatures, and 200 atmospheres of pressure to turn nitrogen and hydrogen into ammonia. With the help of Carl Bosch and BASF, the process was scaled up industrially in 1913 — transforming agriculture forever. Wheat yields doubled, rice production surged, and the Green Revolution was made possible. Nearly half of the nitrogen in your body today comes from food grown with Haber-Bosch fertilizers.

But there’s a dark side. The same ammonia was used to make explosives in World War I, and Haber personally oversaw the first chemical weapon attack with chlorine gas at Ypres in 1915. His work saved billions from starvation yet fueled war and environmental damage. It’s the ultimate double-edged sword of science: the power to feed the world and the power to destroy it.

If you’ve searched for Haber process explained, Fritz Haber biography, Haber Bosch fertilizer, history of fertilizers, Green Revolution, or nitrogen fixation chemistry, this video has you covered.
